You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

[HarnessEntry(id='arc_stamp_motif_on_exact_zero_shape_matches', kind='memory', title='ARC: stamp motif on exact zero-shape matches', content="For ARC grids with a sparse colored motif embedded in a noisy 0/background-color field, a task may ask to find every translation where the motif's colored-cell mask lands entirely on zeros, then recolor those zero cells with the motif color. Preserve the original motif and every nonmatching cell. Match the original orientation only; do not rotate or reflect unless demos show otherwise. Ignore motif bounding-box cells that are not colored: the match condition is that all motif cells land on 0, not that the whole bounding box matches a fixed pattern. Overlapping matches should produce the union of their motif cells. Demonstrated with a 3-colored 4x5 mask: two same-orientation placements on zeros were recolored, including overlaps, and output differences exactly equaled the union. Another 6-cell 1 mask in a 0/9 field had three placements; the output was the motif color at all their cells. Previous examples also confirmed no rotated/reflected matches. Use demos to verify target background, motif color, and whether orientation changes are allowed. Practical caution: transcribing a grid with even one omitted cell can hide a valid match and produce an invalid-sized output; verify every row has the stated width before matching and before submission. Confirmed again in task-58fa3f1c: a sparse 8-cell color-5 mask in a noisy 0/9 grid had exactly two translations whose mask cells were all 0; stamp 5 on both, preserve the original motif and all other cells.

Another accepted instance (task-58fa3f1c): on a 29x11 grid with background 6, scattered zero cells, and an 8-shaped L triomino with mask offsets {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0)}, the rule was to stamp 8 over every translation whose three mask positions were all originally 0. There were 25 placements; preserve all 6s and unmatched 0s and take the union if placements overlap. This confirms the rule also applies when the nonzero background is 6 and the motif has only three colored cells. Compute matches from the original grid, not incrementally from already-stamped cells.

Additional accepted instance (task-58fa3f1c, 16x18): background 0 with scattered color-3 noise and a 7-cell color-2 stencil. In its 3x4 bounding box, the stencil mask offsets (0-indexed) are {(0,0),(0,2),(0,3),(1,1),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2)}. Search all in-bounds translations in the original input and accept one exactly when all seven mask cells are 0; bbox holes are irrelevant. There were 22 placements, with top-lefts (0,7),(0,9),(0,12),(1,3),(1,10),(1,11),(1,12),(3,1),(3,13),(4,2),(5,8),(7,5),(8,0),(8,1),(9,0),(9,1),(11,5),(12,6),(12,7),(12,8),(12,9),(13,6). Recolor the union of their mask cells to 2, preserving original stencil, color-3 noise, and unmatched zeros. Accepted first submission. Reinforces the same-orientation, original-grid mask match across another nonzero stencil color and a denser/asymmetric mask.", path='arc-patterns', scope='global', reference={}, arguments={}, metadata={}, source='agent', created_at='2026-10-20T08:42:09.205188+00:00', updated_at='2026-10-20T12:03:06.182467+00:00', version=5), HarnessEntry(id='arc_task_276f8e5f_extend_markers_toward_edge_bars', kind='memory', title='ARC task-276f8e5f: extend markers toward edge bars', content="For task-276f8e5f, a uniform field has two same-colored perpendicular edge bars in opposite corner regions and sparse cells of another color in the region by one bar. Extend each sparse marker horizontally through the background toward its adjacent edge bar, using the marker color for intervening cells; recolor the original marker to 4. Also copy the row-occupancy pattern of those markers, aligned by row offset within their edge-bar segment, into the opposite edge-bar segment: draw marker-color horizontal rays across that segment from its bar to the far edge on each corresponding row. Preserve the bar cells and all unrelated cells. Demonstration: 15x9 field 5, bars of 8 at right rows0-4 and left rows10-14, sparse 1s at (10,5),(12,3),(13,6),(14,4). Rays from each 1 leftward to the 8 bar recolor each 1 to 4; matching row offsets 0,2,3,4 are filled with 1 across rows0,2,3,4 to the right-side bar, leaving row1 unchanged. Another demo uses left-top/right-bottom bars of 5, sparse 2 markers near right-bottom bar, and does the same with color2. In test task input, rows0-3 col0 are 5, rows6-9 col5 are 5, dots of 2 at (6,1),(7,2),(8,1),(9,1): fill rows0-3 cols1-5 with 2; fill lower rows toward right 5 bar with 2 and turn dots to 4.

Accepted test instance (task-276f8e5f): 11x7 field of 5, zero edge bars at right rows 0–2 (column 6) and left rows 4–6 (column 0), sparse 7 markers at (4,3) and (5,3). Fill rows 0 and 1 across columns 0–5 with 7, preserving the right-edge zeros. Extend each marker leftward: set columns 1–2 to 7 and recolor each original marker at column 3 to 4; preserve left-edge zeros and all other cells. Rows 2 onward otherwise remain unchanged. This output was accepted. The row offsets occupied by the markers in the left bar segment are copied across the opposite segment from its edge bar; original markers become 4.

Accepted 20x19 instance (background 5, bars 6, markers 9): top boundary bar at row 0, cols 9–17; opposite bottom bar at row 19, cols 0–8; markers at (4,14),(7,17),(9,16),(14,13),(17,12). Treat this as the rotated orientation of the edge-bar projection rule: each marker is in the segment aligned with the top bar, so draw a 9 ray vertically upward from row 1 to just before its marker, recolor the marker to 4, and leave cells beyond it unchanged. Copy marker column offsets relative to the top bar's left endpoint (cols 12–17 offsets 3,4,5,7,8) to the opposite bottom bar segment (cols 3,4,5,7,8); draw 9 upward from row 18 through row 0 in those columns, preserving both 6 bars. This output was accepted. Bar segment alignment uses left-to-right offset, even though the bars occupy opposite halves.

Accepted 24x27 instance (background 3, edge bars 9, marker color 7): right bar at col 26 rows 2–11 and left bar at col 0 rows 14–23; markers at (2,11),(3,23),(4,17),(6,23),(8,3),(11,15). Each marker lies in the right-bar segment: draw 7 rightward through the cells before col 26, and change the original marker to 4. Their row offsets 0,1,2,4,6,9 map to rows 14,15,16,18,20,23 of the opposite left-bar segment; fill columns 1–26 with 7 on those rows, preserving col 0 bar. This exact test output was accepted.

Accepted 24x27 instance (background 3, edge bars 9, marker color 7): right bar at col 26 rows 2–11 and left bar at col 0 rows 14–23; markers at (2,11),(3,23),(4,17),(6,23),(8,3),(11,15). Each marker lies in the right-bar segment: draw 7 rightward through the cells before col 26, and change the original marker to 4. Their row offsets 0,1,2,4,6,9 map to rows 14,15,16,18,20,23 of the opposite left-bar segment; fill columns 1–26 with 7 on those rows, preserving col 0 bar. This exact test output was accepted.

Endpoint note: projected rays reach and include the far grid edge outside the opposite bar (but never overwrite actual bar cells); local marker rays stop before the original marker, which becomes 4. Do not truncate opposite-edge projections one cell early.
", path='general', scope='global', reference={}, arguments={}, metadata={}, source='agent', created_at='2026-10-20T09:03:56.789050+00:00', updated_at='2026-10-20T13:26:58.339270+00:00', version=6), HarnessEntry(id='arc_task_276f8e5f_project_boundary_dominoes_toward_opposite_edge', kind='memory', title='ARC task-276f8e5f: connect boundary-bar offsets to markers and opposite edge', content="For task-276f8e5f with horizontal boundary bars (top and bottom rows), use each bar as a column segment. The sparse marker pixels lie between a boundary bar and the grid interior on the same columns as that bar. For each marker, draw its marker-color ray from the adjacent boundary bar toward the marker, stopping just before it; recolor the original marker to 4. Also map each marker's column offset within its adjacent bar to the corresponding offset within the opposite bar, and project that opposite-bar cell through the interior to the far boundary using the marker color. Preserve both bars, all cells beyond each marker on its local ray, and all unrelated cells. When the bars occupy different columns, offsets are left-to-right within the bar segments (e.g. offset 0 in top segment maps to offset 0 in bottom segment). This describes both the marker-local rays and the full rays projected from the opposite bar; do not draw only a ray from one arbitrary endpoint.

Accepted demo (12x8): background 0; top bar color 6 at row 0, cols 5–7; bottom bar at row 11, cols 0–2; marker 1 at (2,7). Draw 1 at (1,7), change marker (2,7) to 4, and project the matching offset 2 from the bottom bar upward in col 2, rows 0–10. Preserve bars/background.

Accepted test (14x11): background 7; top bar color 2 at row 0, cols 3–5; bottom bar at row 13, cols 0–2; marker 3s at (3,4), (7,3), (7,5). Local rays from the top bar fill (1–2, col 4), (1–6, col 3), and (1–6, col 5); replace each original marker with 4. Project their offsets 1,0,2 from the bottom bar as full 3 rays in cols 1,0,2, rows 0–12. Preserve both bars and all other cells. This submission was accepted.

Earlier confirmed examples following the same rule: (a) background 7, top 8-bar at cols 14–15 and bottom 8-bar at cols 9–10, marker 3 at row 3 col 9: project offset 0 from the top bar down col 14 to the bottom edge; draw upward from bottom-bar col 9 to just before the marker, then change marker to 4. (b) background 9, top 0-bar cols 3–4 and bottom 0-bar cols 16–17, marker 1 at row 5 col 3: project offset 0 from bottom bar upward in col 16 to the top edge; draw downward from top-bar col 3 to just before the marker; change marker to 4. Marker recolor is always 4, not input-color+1.

Rotated cases with vertical boundary bars are handled by swapping rows/columns: rays run horizontally, and marker row offsets map between opposite edge segments. A related accepted example: background 5; right-edge color-8 bar in rows 0–4, left-edge bar rows 10–14; sparse 1 markers at (10,5),(12,3),(13,6),(14,4). Local rays go rightward from each marker toward the adjacent left bar; markers become 4. Matching row offsets 0,2,3,4 are projected across the opposite right-side segment (rows 0,2,3,4), leaving row 1 unchanged. Preserve bars and unrelated cells.

Accepted test (25x6, background 6, bar/marker color setup): top-right boundary bar color 3 at rows 0–3, col 5; opposite bottom-left bar color 3 at rows 19–22, col 0; color-7 markers at (20,3),(21,4),(22,2). Project marker offsets 1,2,3 from the lower bar segment to top rows 1,2,3: fill columns 0–4 with 7 on each of rows 1–3, preserving col 5 bar. Extend each bottom marker leftward toward col 0: on row 20 fill cols 1–2 with 7 and recolor marker col 3 to 4; on row 21 fill cols 1–3 with 7 and recolor col 4 to 4; on row 22 fill col 1 with 7 and recolor col 2 to 4. Preserve all bars and other background cells. This instance was accepted on the first submission.

Important endpoint nuance confirmed on a 29x8 test: projected rays from the opposite boundary segment include the far grid edge, even in cells outside that edge's bar (e.g. a top bar at row 0 projects down through row 28 inclusive; preserve only the actual bar cells). A first answer that stopped projected rows at 27 was rejected; extending the two projected columns into row 28 fixed it. In contrast, local rays from the adjacent bar stop immediately before the marker, the marker becomes 4, and cells beyond the marker toward the far side stay unchanged. This was confirmed by demos where projected rays fill the opposite boundary row/column outside its bar, while local rays only fill the gap between marker and adjacent bar.

Three fresh demos in this instance confirmed the same stripe-count period rule (N=6, 6, and 5).', path='general', scope='global', reference={}, arguments={}, metadata={}, source='agent', created_at='2026-10-20T12:10:28.503596+00:00', updated_at='2026-10-20T13:23:10.766713+00:00', version=3), HarnessEntry(id='arc_task_2fd86235_decode_uniform_corner_cells_in_stripe_grid', kind='memory', title='ARC task-2fd86235: decode uniform-corner cells in stripe grid', content="For ARC task-2fd86235, the input is a regular lattice/grid of large uniform-color cells whose divider lines are mostly one color. Some divider intersections are recolored with marker colors. Find the bounding box of all non-background marker junctions on the lattice. The output has one cell per lattice rectangle between consecutive junction rows/columns inside that marker bbox. Set an output cell to marker color X only when all four corner junctions of that rectangle are X; otherwise use the large interior fill color. Ignore rectangles outside the marker bounding box. This is confirmed by demos: e.g. a 1 color 2x2 set of junctions produces one 1 output cell, while incomplete/mixed corner rectangles remain fill color; marker runs can create adjoining same-color output cells when all four corners match. For the test instance, nodes rows 3,6,9,12,15,18 and cols 2,8,14,20,26 yielded 5x4 output [[7,7,0,0],[5,7,7,7],[5,5,7,9],[7,5,7,9],[7,5,7,9]]. Key pitfall: do NOT color an output cell merely because top/one edge endpoints match; require all four corners. Determine crop as min/max marker junction bbox, output dimensions are intervals between those lattice lines.

Accepted test instance (24x28): lattice junction lines at rows 0,5,10,15,20 and columns 0,6,12,18,24; separator color 3, broad cell fill 2. Junction colors by row were [3,3,3,7,7], [6,6,3,7,7], [6,6,3,3,3], [3,1,1,8,8], [3,1,1,8,8]. Applying the all-four-corners-same-marker rule within the marker junction bbox gives accepted 4x4 output [[2,2,2,7],[6,2,2,2],[2,2,2,2],[2,1,2,8]].

Additional accepted test (20x26): horizontal junction rows 0, 8, 16 and the marker-bbox columns 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23 produce node matrix [[5,5,2,2,3,3],[5,5,5,5,3,3],[2,2,5,5,2,2]]. The broad interior fill is 9. Requiring all four corners of each cell to match yields accepted output [[5,9,9,9,3],[9,9,5,9,9]]. A separate demo confirms unmatched/mixed corner cells use the broad interior fill (e.g. 7), while a same-color four-corner cell is copied to output.

Non-9 marker junction bbox spans rows 7..22 and columns 3..27, so use the six junction rows [7,10,13,16,19,22] and seven junction columns [3,7,11,15,19,23,27] to form a 5x6 output. The node-color matrix is [[9,9,9,4,4,3,3],[5,5,4,4,4,3,3],[5,5,4,4,8,8,9],[5,5,9,9,8,8,8],[4,4,7,7,8,8,8],[4,4,7,7,8,8,9]]. As usual, output marker color only when all four corners match; otherwise fill 1. Accepted output: [[1,1,1,4,1,3],[5,1,4,1,1,1],[5,1,1,1,8,1],[1,1,1,1,8,8],[4,1,7,1,8,1]].
